claims.text: DIA Info Memo U-09-2660 (13 Nov 2009) frames the two names as the same thing: it evaluates 'a request from Senator Harry Reid (enclosure 1) to establish a restricted special access program (SAP) for the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Application Program Contract, referred to in Senator Reid's letter as the Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program (AAITP).'

The DIA release consistently spells it 'AAITP' (Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program) in 2009 documents, not the later-familiar 'AATIP'. The USD(I) memorandum subject line reads: 'Senator Harry Reid's Request to Put the Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program (AAITP) under Special Access Protection'.

DIA Read Ahead for the 19 Nov 2009 meeting states the DIA position: 'the content of the deliverables from the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Application Program contract, referred to by Senator Reid as the AATIP, for FY09 and those expected in FY10, do not meet the criteria as specified in DoD 5200.1-R to justify the additional protection provided by a SAP.'
AARO Vol. I records that AAWSAP 'was also known [as] AATIP' and that DIA cancelled the program in 2012; supporters then proposed a follow-on program, KONA BLUE, to DHS, which DHS rejected.

The concealment-relevant fact is not that AATIP was fake but that it was administratively real and deliberately kept out of SAP channels. DIA's own recommendation against a SAP (Nov 2009) is what later allowed officials to characterise AATIP as low-significance: a program denied special protection leaves no SAP paper trail to point at.

AARO Historical Record Report Vol. I states: 'Unlike AAWSAP, AATIP was never an official DoD program. However, after AAWSAP was cancelled, the AATIP moniker was used by some individuals associated with an informal, unofficial UAP community of interest within DoD that researched UAP sightings from military observers as part of their ancillary job duties.'

AARO's formulation is the load-bearing denial artifact: it concedes an actual DoD community of interest researching military UAP sightings, then denies it program status on a naming technicality. DIA's own 2009 correspondence uses 'AAITP' and 'AAWSAP' interchangeably for the same contract, so the 'never an official DoD program' line depends entirely on which of the two names is treated as canonical.

claims.text: The DIA FOIA Electronic Reading Room posts 37 files whose names begin 'Defense_Intelligence_Reference_Document_'. 32 of those have been retrieved and their cover pages transcribed; DIA document numbers, publication dates and Intelligence Cut-Off Dates are recorded on the individual document nodes.

The DIRDs fall into two DIA series banners printed on the cover: 'Acquisition Threat Support' (the FY2009 tranche, ICOD 1 December 2009, published Dec 2009 - Apr 2010) and 'Defense Futures' (the FY2010 tranche, ICOD Jul-Dec 2010, published Nov 2010 - Jan 2011).

DIA document numbers follow the pattern DIA-08-YYMM-NNN, where 08 ties to the FY2008 program start and YYMM is the production month — e.g. DIA-08-0911-016 (Nov 2009), DIA-08-1003-015 (Mar 2010), DIA-08-1102-007 (Feb 2011 batch). The numbering is sparse in the released set, which indicates the released DIRDs are not the complete numbered series.

DIA Info Memo U-429-09 Enclosure 1 lists the 26 FY2009 technical reports by working title (not final DIRD title), including several never released as DIRDs under those names: 'Pulse-Power-Based Weaponry', 'Space-Time Modifications for Spaceflight Applications', 'Novel MEMS-Based Biosensors', 'Metamaterials for Aerospace Applications', 'Metallic Glasses', 'Metallic Spintronics', 'Materials for Advanced Aerospace Platforms', 'Wormholes in Space Time', 'Gravity Wave Communication', 'Vacuum Energy Applications', 'Improved Statistical Approach to Drake Equation', 'Maverick vs. Corporate Research Cultures', 'Warp Drives', 'Controlling Devices Without Limb-Operated Interfaces', 'Field Effects on Biological Tissues', 'High-Energy Laser Weapon', 'Quantum Entanglement Communications', 'Space Access: Where Been, Where Go', 'Advanced Nuclear Propulsion for Deep Space', 'Inertial Electrostatic Confinement Fusion', 'Theory and Experiments of Invisibility Cloaking', 'Superconductors in Gravity Research', 'Antigravity for Aerospace Applications', 'Positron Aerospace Propulsion', 'Biosensors and BioMEMS', 'Programmable Matter'.

In the DIA-released copies every DIRD author is withheld under FOIA exemption (b)(6) and the 'Prepared by' office under (b)(3) 10 USC 424. Two author surnames survive uncensored inside the review excerpts of Info Memo U-429-09: 'Hathaway' (The Role of Superconductors in Gravity Research) and 'Tsoi' (Metallic Spintronics).

That two surnames survive the redaction pass in U-429-09 while every cover page is scrubbed indicates redaction was applied by template rather than by review, and that DIA's own reviewers wrote about these authors by name in internal correspondence. Author identities are therefore recoverable from the released corpus itself, not only from leaks.

Confirmed unreachable in this pass: 5 of the 37 DIRD filenames listed by DIA have no resolvable FileId URL — Biomaterials; Materials_For_Advanced_Aerospace_Platforms; Metallic_Glasses_For_Aerospace_Applications; Metallic_Spintronics; Metamaterials_For_Aerospace_Applications. The complete Wayback CDX index for dia.mil FOIA reading-room FileId URLs (3,536 unique FileIds) contains no snapshot of them, and the live page does not expose FileIds to a text fetcher.

Describes contractor activity including reviewing new UFO cases and older Project BLUE BOOK cases, operating debriefing and investigatory teams, and examining purportedly recovered materials.
Records that after DIA ended AAWSAP in 2012, supporters proposed a follow-on program, KONA BLUE, to the Department of Homeland Security, which DHS rejected.

AARO's report is itself an artifact of the concealment posture it purports to close out: it confirms the appropriation, the program, the contractor activity and the attempted transfer to DHS, while declining to name the contractor, the program manager, or the DIRD authors — the same redaction boundary DIA drew in the FOIA release.

On KONA BLUE: it 'traces its origins to the DIA-managed AAWSAP/AATIP program'; supporters 'proposed to DHS that they create and fund a new version of AAWSAP/AATIP under a SAP', eventually submitting 'a Prospective Special Access Program (PSAP)' which was 'rejected by DHS leadership for lacking merit'.
AARO characterises the KONA BLUE proposal as one that 'would restart UAP investigations, paranormal research...and reverse-engineer any recovered off-world spacecraft'.
Report title: 'Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), Volume I', dated February 2024, Volume I approximately 45 pages.

AARO confirms in an official report that a proposal to 'reverse-engineer any recovered off-world spacecraft' was formally submitted to DHS as a Prospective Special Access Program by people who had run the DIA program. A PSAP submission is a bureaucratic instrument, not a rumour: it means the recovery premise was carried into formal special-access channels twice (Reid's 2009 SAP request, and KONA BLUE), and was refused both times on merit/classification grounds rather than on the grounds that the subject matter was fictitious.
